title: Shaded Versions of Shared Vocabulary Types
pattern: Multiple versions of the same library are isolated by renaming/shading them into one binary even though their vocabulary types must cross the same API boundaries, patching over a version conflict instead of migrating the shared types.
why_bad: Shading only works for isolated function calls. Renaming cannot make distinct type identities interchangeable: the moment a type from one shaded version is passed to code expecting the other, the result is a compile-time mismatch or runtime failure, and the workaround leaves conversion debt at interfaces, masks real design debt, and bloats the binary.
detection:
The linter must observe both:
1. Multiple major versions of the same package imported in a single module or build configuration (renamed/shaded dependencies).
2. Those versions exchanging vocabulary types across an interface boundary between distinct modules — either directly (a value of one version's type passed where the other version's type is expected) or via application-side mapping wrappers forced to translate types from version A to version B.
counterexample:
`Context-dependent`
Shading a self-contained dependency whose types never leave its wrapper (e.g. a JSON parsing library whose types never exit the wrapping service). A supported transition that re-exports the same canonical types, such as a correctly applied semver trick:
```toml
# Valid: semver trick re-exports common types seamlessly
[dependencies]
libbase = "2.0.0"
```
fix:
Converge the exchanging components on one compatible version of the vocabulary dependency and migrate callers, enforcing the One-Version Rule across the repository. Where supported, use a semver-trick release to preserve type identity during the transition.
```toml
[dependencies]
libbase = "2.0.0"
```
source:
- Titus Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* (2020) [320, 338]
- Jon Gjengset, *Rust for Rustaceans* (2021) [578]; *Software Engineering at Google (Winters et al.), Chapter 16, p. 341 [143, 989]*
